title: Redundant Connection II
summary: Given a directed graph that originally formed a rooted tree with one additional directed edge, identify and return an edge that can be removed to restore the graph as a rooted tree with n nodes.
statement: Given a directed graph that originally formed a rooted tree with one additional directed edge, identify and return an edge that can be removed to restore the graph as a rooted tree with n nodes. If multiple edges meet this criterion, return the one that appears last in the input array.
constraints: A rooted directed tree on n nodes has one extra directed edge.
Remove one edge to restore a rooted tree; when multiple answers work, return the one occurring last.
reference_solution:
def redundant_directed_edge(edges):
    n=len(edges); parent_of=[0]*(n+1); first=second=None
    for edge in edges:
        parent,child=edge
        if parent_of[child]: first=[parent_of[child],child];second=edge
        else: parent_of[child]=parent
    parent=list(range(n+1))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x]!=x:
            parent[x]=parent[parent[x]];x=parent[x]
        return x
    for edge in edges:
        if edge is second: continue
        left,right=edge;a,b=find(left),find(right)
        if a==b:return first if first else edge
        parent[b]=a
    return second
hints: The extra edge creates either a cycle, a node with two parents, or both.
Record the two-parent candidates, then run union-find while skipping the later candidate.
On a remaining cycle choose the earlier parent edge; otherwise choose the skipped later edge.
These cases exhaust the two ways a rooted-tree invariant can fail: indegree and acyclicity.
editorial: These cases exhaust the two ways a rooted-tree invariant can fail: indegree and acyclicity.
